books.title: Kalila and Dimna
books.author: Ibn al-Muqaffa
books.desc: Two jackals at a lion's court tell fable after fable about friendship, ambition and betrayal — the Arabic masterpiece of animal tales, in its original language.
about: Kalila and Dimna is a collection of fables framed as the advice a wise philosopher, Bidpai, gives to an Indian king. Its heart is the story of two jackals, Kalila and Dimna, at the court of a lion: Dimna's scheming to win the king's favour sets off a chain of intrigue, and each character answers the others with a story of its own.

The fables descend from the Sanskrit Panchatantra, which passed into Middle Persian and was rendered into Arabic around 750 by Abd Allah Ibn al-Muqaffa. His clear, elegant prose made the book a model of Arabic style, and it travelled on into Hebrew, Latin, Spanish and many other languages, reaching La Fontaine in seventeenth-century France.
This edition presents the Arabic text.
books.author_short: Abd Allah Ibn al-Muqaffa (c. 724–759) was a Persian-born writer and translator whose Arabic prose became a model of the language.
books.author_long: Abd Allah Ibn al-Muqaffa (c. 724–759) was born in Persia and worked as a secretary for governors under the late Umayyads and early Abbasids. He translated Middle Persian works into Arabic and wrote books of advice for rulers. His Kalila and Dimna is counted among the founding works of Arabic literary prose. He was executed in Basra while still in his thirties.

books.title: Hayy ibn Yaqdhan
books.author: Ibn Tufayl
books.desc: A child grows up alone on a desert island and, by observation and reason alone, rises to knowledge of nature and of God — the philosophical novel of Muslim Spain.
about: Hayy ibn Yaqdhan ("Alive, son of Awake") tells of a boy raised by a gazelle on an uninhabited island. With no language and no teacher, he studies the animals, dissects his dead foster mother to understand life, learns to use fire and tools, and climbs step by step from the physical world to astronomy, metaphysics and mystical contemplation.

Ibn Tufayl, court physician to the Almohad caliph in Marrakesh, wrote the tale in the twelfth century to show that unaided reason can reach the same truths as revelation. Translated into Latin in 1671 and soon into English, it was read widely in Enlightenment Europe and is often cited among the ancestors of Robinson Crusoe.
This edition presents the Arabic text.
books.author_short: Ibn Tufayl (c. 1105–1185) was an Andalusian philosopher and physician at the Almohad court in Marrakesh.
books.author_long: Abu Bakr Ibn Tufayl (c. 1105–1185) was born near Granada and served as physician and adviser to the Almohad caliph Abu Yaqub Yusuf in Marrakesh. He introduced the young Ibn Rushd (Averroes) to the caliph, encouraging his commentaries on Aristotle. Hayy ibn Yaqdhan is his only surviving work.

books.title: The Ring of the Dove
books.author: Ibn Hazm
books.desc: A treatise on love written in Córdoba a thousand years ago — its signs, its messengers, its secrets and its sorrows, told through anecdotes and verse.
about: The Ring of the Dove (Tawq al-Hamama) is a book about love and lovers, written around 1022 by the Andalusian scholar Ibn Hazm at the request of a friend. In thirty chapters he describes love's nature and causes, the signs that betray it, falling in love from a description or at first sight, the go-between, the jealous watcher, union and separation, faithfulness and betrayal.

Each chapter mixes reflection with stories from the author's own life and from people he knew in Córdoba, and with poems he composed himself. It is one of the most personal works of medieval Arabic literature and a vivid picture of Andalusian society in the last years of the Umayyad caliphate.
This edition presents the Arabic text.
books.author_short: Ibn Hazm (994–1064) was an Andalusian poet, historian, jurist and philosopher from Córdoba.
books.author_long: Ali ibn Ahmad Ibn Hazm (994–1064) was born in Córdoba into a family close to the Umayyad court. After the fall of the caliphate he was imprisoned and exiled several times and turned to scholarship, writing on law, theology, history, comparative religion and ethics. He is remembered both as a leading thinker of the Zahiri school of law and as the author of The Ring of the Dove.

books.title: The Travels of Ibn Battuta
books.author: Ibn Battuta
books.desc: A young man from Tangier sets out for Mecca in 1325 and keeps travelling for almost thirty years — to Cairo, Constantinople, India, China and Timbuktu.
about: In 1325 Ibn Battuta, a twenty-one-year-old from Tangier, left home to perform the pilgrimage to Mecca. He did not return for nearly three decades. His journeys took him across North Africa and the Middle East, to East Africa, Anatolia, the Golden Horde, Central Asia and India, where he served as a judge in Delhi, then to the Maldives, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia and China, and finally to Al-Andalus and across the Sahara to Mali.

Back in Morocco, he dictated his memories to the scholar Ibn Juzayy at the order of Sultan Abu Inan. The resulting book, A Gift to Those Who Contemplate the Wonders of Cities and the Marvels of Travelling (1355), is one of the great travel narratives of any age, full of rulers, saints, markets, customs and dangers on the road.
This edition presents the Arabic text.
books.author_short: Ibn Battuta (1304–c. 1369) was a Moroccan traveller who journeyed for almost thirty years across Africa and Asia.
books.author_long: Muhammad Ibn Battuta (1304–c. 1369) was born in Tangier into a family of Muslim jurists. Setting out for Mecca in 1325, he travelled some 120,000 kilometres over the next three decades, through most of the Islamic world and beyond. On his return to Fez he dictated his account to Ibn Juzayy; it remains a major source on the fourteenth-century world.
